title: Μοχλὸς καὶ κριός
titleEn: The Stake and the Ram — Odyssey 9.371–474
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his story at the Phaeacian court, goes on from the moment the drunken Cyclops falls asleep. He thrusts the olive-wood stake into the ashes, and when it is about to catch fire he and four companions drive it into the Cyclops' one eye and twist it round, as a man twirls a drill; the eye hisses like iron plunged in water. The Cyclops howls and tears the stake out, and the other Cyclopes come to ask what is wrong. When he answers that Nobody is killing him by a trick or by force, they tell him to pray to his father Poseidon and go away, and Odysseus laughs to himself at the trick of the name. The blinded Cyclops sits in the doorway groping for any man who might slip out, and Odysseus ties his companions under the bellies of the rams, three rams to a man, and clings to the fleece of the best ram himself. At dawn the flocks go out, and the Cyclops feels their backs and never notices the men underneath; he speaks to the lead ram, who goes last, and wishes it could tell him where Nobody is hiding. Once clear of the yard, Odysseus frees himself and his men, they drive the flocks to the ship, hold back the men's weeping, and row out to sea. When they are as far off as a shout will carry, Odysseus begins to taunt the Cyclops.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ ἀνακλινθεὶς πέσεν ὕπτιος, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
κεῖτ’ ἀποδοχμώσας παχὺν αὐχένα, κὰδ δέ μιν ὕπνος
ᾕρει πανδαμάτωρ·
sentences.tr:
ē kai anaklintheis pesen hyptios, autar epeita
keit’ apodochmōsas pachyn auchena, kad de min hypnos
hēirei pandamatōr·
sentences.i: He spoke, and leaning back he fell over on his back, and then he lay with his thick neck bent to one side, and all-subduing sleep took hold of him;
sentences.n: ἦ καί 'he spoke, and' closes the Cyclops' speech of the previous part. Odysseus is still the narrator, so only the speeches of others are in quotation marks. πέσεν is ἔπεσεν with no augment, and κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο 'lay'. ἀποδοχμώσας 'bending sideways' is a rare verb, taken from its use here. κὰδ … ᾕρει is one verb pulled apart (tmesis): κατά, with its last vowel lost and τ assimilated to δ, plus ᾕρει, the imperfect of αἱρέω 'take'; the sense is 'took him down', that is, overcame him. πανδαμάτωρ is 'all-subduing', from πᾶν and δαμάω 'tame, overpower'.

sentences.t:
φάρυγος δ’ ἐξέσσυτο οἶνος
ψωμοί τ’ ἀνδρόμεοι·
sentences.tr:
pharygos d’ exessyto oinos
psōmoi t’ andromeoi·
sentences.l:
and from his gullet rushed out wine
and human morsels;
sentences.i: and from his gullet wine came rushing out, and morsels of human flesh;
sentences.n: φάρυγος is the genitive of φάρυγξ 'gullet', here 'from the gullet'. ἐξέσσυτο 'rushed out' is the aorist of σεύομαι 'rush', whose stem doubles its σ. ψωμοί are 'morsels, bits of food'; ἀνδρόμεοι is the adjective 'human, of a man', the same word as in the ἀνδρόμεα κρέα 'human flesh' of the previous part. So the wine and the flesh come up together.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἐρεύγετο οἰνοβαρείων.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ereugeto oinobareiōn.
sentences.l: and he belched, heavy with wine.
sentences.i: and he belched, weighed down with wine.
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun 'he'. ἐρεύγετο is 'belched', and the word also covers spewing out what was eaten. οἰνοβαρείων 'heavy with wine' is the participle of a verb built on οἶνος and βαρύς; this is its only use in this part.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼ τὸν μοχλὸν ὑπὸ σποδοῦ ἤλασα πολλῆς,
ἧος θερμαίνοιτο·
sentences.tr:
kai tot’ egō ton mochlon hypo spodou ēlasa pollēs,
hēos thermainoito·
sentences.l:
And then I the stake under ash thrust, much of it,
until it should be heated;
sentences.i: Then I thrust the stake in under a great deal of ash, until it should grow hot;
sentences.n: τὸν μοχλόν is the stake of the previous part, here heated for the blinding. ἤλασα is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive, thrust', and σποδοῦ πολλῆς is 'much ash', a genitive with ὑπό. ἧος is the epic form of ἕως 'until', and the optative θερμαίνοιτο 'should get hot' says what was to happen, not what did.

sentences.t:
ἔπεσσι δὲ πάντας ἑταίρους
θάρσυνον, μή τίς μοι ὑποδείσας ἀναδύη.
sentences.tr:
epessi de pantas hetairous
tharsynon, mē tis moi hypodeisas anadyē.
sentences.l:
and with words all my companions
I heartened, lest some one, for me, through fear, draw back.
sentences.i: and I heartened all my companions with words, so that none of them, out of fear, should draw back on me.
sentences.n: ἔπεσσι 'with words' is a dative plural in -εσσι. θάρσυνον is the imperfect of θαρσύνω 'encourage', with no augment. μή with the aorist optative ἀναδύη (the subjunctive would be spelled ἀναδύῃ) expresses fear or purpose after the past tense θάρσυνον: 'lest anyone back out'. ἀναδύομαι means 'come up out of the water' and so 'retreat, shrink back'; μοι 'for me' is the dative of the person who would suffer.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τάχ’ ὁ μοχλὸς ἐλάινος ἐν πυρὶ μέλλεν
ἅψεσθαι, χλωρός περ ἐών, διεφαίνετο δ’ αἰνῶς,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἆσσον φέρον ἐκ πυρός, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
ἵσταντ’·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tach’ ho mochlos elainos en pyri mellen
hapsesthai, chlōros per eōn, diephaineto d’ ainōs,
kai tot’ egōn asson pheron ek pyros, amphi d’ hetairoi
histant’·
sentences.l:
But when presently the stake, the olive-wood one, in the fire was about
to catch, though being green, and it glowed terribly,
then I nearer carried it from the fire, and round, companions
stood;
sentences.i: But when the olive-wood stake, green though it was, was just about to catch fire, and glowed terribly, then I carried it closer, out of the fire, and my companions stood around;
sentences.n: One long sentence: ὅτε … μέλλεν 'when it was about to', then καὶ τότε 'then' answers it. μέλλεν is ἔμελλεν with no augment, and ἅψεσθαι is the infinitive 'to catch fire'. χλωρός is 'green', unseasoned wood, and περ ἐών 'though it was' concedes that green wood should not burn. διεφαίνετο 'shone through' is taken as 'glowed'; αἰνῶς is 'terribly'. ἆσσον is the comparative 'nearer'. ἵσταντ’ is ἵσταντο 'took their stand', from the middle of ἵστημι.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ θάρσος ἐνέπνευσεν μέγα δαίμων.
sentences.tr: autar tharsos enepneusen mega daimōn.
sentences.l: but courage great a power breathed into (us).
sentences.i: but some power breathed great courage into us.
sentences.n: δαίμων is 'a divine power', left unnamed, as it often is when something happens that a man cannot account for. ἐνέπνευσεν 'breathed into' has the object θάρσος 'courage', with μέγα 'great' agreeing with it. The Greek names no one who receives the courage, so 'us' is supplied: the men and Odysseus together. The unit begins mid-line, at αὐτὰρ 'but'.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν μοχλὸν ἑλόντες ἐλάινον, ὀξὺν ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ,
ὀφθαλμῷ ἐνέρεισαν·
sentences.tr:
hoi men mochlon helontes elainon, oxyn ep’ akrōi,
ophthalmōi enereisan·
sentences.l:
They, the stake having taken, the olive-wood one, sharp at the tip,
in the eye drove in;
sentences.i: They took the olive-wood stake, sharp at its tip, and drove it into his eye;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν 'they' is the four chosen men (οἱ is the pronoun, not the article); the contrast is with ἐγὼ δέ in the next unit. ἐλάινον is the adjective 'of olive-wood', from ἐλαία. ἐνέρεισαν is the aorist of ἐνερείδω 'press in, thrust in'. ὀφθαλμῷ is a singular dative, 'in the eye': the Cyclops has one.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐφύπερθεν ἐρεισθεὶς
δίνεον, ὡς ὅτε τις τρυπῷ δόρυ νήιον ἀνὴρ
τρυπάνῳ, οἱ δέ τ’ ἔνερθεν ὑποσσείουσιν ἱμάντι
ἁψάμενοι ἑκάτερθε, τὸ δὲ τρέχει ἐμμενὲς αἰεί.
sentences.tr:
egō d’ ephyperthen ereistheis
dineon, hōs hote tis trypōi dory nēion anēr
trypanōi, hoi de t’ enerthen hyposseiousin himanti
hapsamenoi hekaterthe, to de trechei emmenes aiei.
sentences.l:
and I, from above, leaning on it,
kept twirling it, as when a man bores a ship’s timber
with a drill, and those below keep shaking it with a strap
having taken hold on either side, and it runs on continuously, always.
sentences.i: and I, leaning on it from above, twirled it, as when a man bores a ship’s timber with a drill while others below keep it spinning with a strap, taking hold of it on either side, and the drill runs on without a stop.
sentences.n: A simile: ὡς ὅτε with the subjunctive τρυπῷ 'as when a man bores' describes a habit, not one event. δίνεον is the imperfect of δινέω 'whirl', uncontracted, and ἐρεισθείς is 'pressing my weight on it'. δόρυ νήιον is 'timber for a ship', νήιος being Ionic for 'of a ship'. τρύπανον is the drill, and the men below ὑποσσείουσιν 'shake from underneath' (the drill is understood as the object) ἱμάντι 'with a strap', a dative of means, ἁψάμενοι ἑκάτερθε 'taking hold on either side' leaves its object unsaid; τὸ δέ is the drill. ἐμμενές means 'continuously'; αἰεί 'always' is Attic ἀεί.

sentences.t:
ὣς τοῦ ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ πυριήκεα μοχλὸν ἑλόντες
δινέομεν, τὸν δ’ αἷμα περίρρεε θερμὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
hōs tou en ophthalmōi pyriēkea mochlon helontes
dineomen, ton d’ haima perirree thermon eonta.
sentences.l:
So in his eye the fire-pointed stake having taken
we twirled it, and round it blood flowed, it being hot.
sentences.i: So we took the fire-pointed stake and twirled it in his eye, and blood flowed round it, hot as it was.
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile: 'so it was with us'. πυριήκεα is 'fire-pointed', built on πῦρ 'fire' and the ἀκ- 'point' of ἀκή; the second half of the word is not fully certain, and the sense fits the stake hardened in fire in the previous part. τοῦ … ὀφθαλμῷ is 'in his eye', τοῦ being a pronoun. τόν in the second line is the stake, and θερμὸν ἐόντα agrees with it, so the stake is hot; περίρρεε is περιέρρεε, 'flowed around', with no augment and uncontracted. δινέομεν is the uncontracted present, a vivid present that English renders 'we twirled'.

sentences.t:
πάντα δέ οἱ βλέφαρ’ ἀμφὶ καὶ ὀφρύας εὗσεν ἀυτμὴ
γλήνης καιομένης, σφαραγεῦντο δέ οἱ πυρὶ ῥίζαι.
sentences.tr:
panta de hoi blephar’ amphi kai ophryas heusen aytmē
glēnēs kaiomenēs, spharageunto de hoi pyri rhizai.
sentences.l:
And all his eyelids round and eyebrows singed the blast
of the eyeball burning, and crackled for him in the fire the roots.
sentences.i: The blast of the burning eyeball singed all his eyelids and his eyebrows round about, and its roots crackled in the fire.
sentences.n: ἀμφί stands between its two nouns: βλέφαρα … ἀμφὶ καὶ ὀφρύας 'round the eyelids and the eyebrows'. εὗσεν is the aorist of εὕω 'singe', and ἀυτμή is 'blast, hot breath'. γλήνη is the eyeball, or the pupil of it. σφαραγεῦντο 'crackled' is the same verb that is said of the udders at 440, where they are 'near bursting'; it is a word for a sound of bursting or cracking. ῥίζαι 'roots' are perhaps the fibres at the back of the eye; the Greek says only 'roots'. The two οἱ are the pronoun 'his'.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ χαλκεὺς πέλεκυν μέγαν ἠὲ σκέπαρνον
εἰν ὕδατι ψυχρῷ βάπτῃ μεγάλα ἰάχοντα
φαρμάσσων·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ anēr chalkeus pelekyn megan ēe skeparnon
ein hydati psychrōi baptēi megala iachonta
pharmassōn·
sentences.i: As when a smith plunges a great axe or an adze into cold water, and it shrieks loudly as he tempers it;
sentences.n: Another simile, whose 'so' comes in the next unit. The simile is the smith hardening iron. ὡς ὅτε with βάπτῃ (subjunctive) again marks a general situation, and εἰν is ἐν. βάπτω is 'dip'. μεγάλα ἰάχοντα 'crying out loudly' is the sound of the hot metal; ἰάχω is used of cries and shouts. φαρμάσσων is a verb of treating with a drug, used here of tempering metal; the sense is taken from the context. An ano teleia falls inside line 393, after φαρμάσσων, and ends this unit.

sentences.t:
τὸ γὰρ αὖτε σιδήρου γε κράτος ἐστίν
ὣς τοῦ σίζ’ ὀφθαλμὸς ἐλαϊνέῳ περὶ μοχλῷ.
sentences.tr:
to gar aute sidērou ge kratos estin
hōs tou siz’ ophthalmos elaïneōi peri mochlōi.
sentences.l:
for that, in turn, of iron indeed the strength is;
so of him hissed the eye about the olive-wood stake.
sentences.i: for that is the strength of iron; so his eye hissed around the olive-wood stake.
sentences.n: τὸ … κράτος ἐστίν is an aside explaining why the smith does it: quenching is what gives iron its strength, κράτος. αὖτε 'in turn' and γε are particles that carry little here. ὣς answers ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ of the previous unit. σίζ’ is σίζε 'hissed', with no augment. τοῦ … ὀφθαλμός is 'his eye', with τοῦ a pronoun, and ἐλαϊνέῳ is the uncontracted form of 'of olive-wood'. The stake is thus compared to the hot iron, and the eye to the water.

sentences.t:
σμερδαλέον δὲ μέγ’ ᾤμωξεν, περὶ δ’ ἴαχε πέτρη,
ἡμεῖς δὲ δείσαντες ἀπεσσύμεθ’·
sentences.tr:
smerdaleon de meg’ ōimōxen, peri d’ iache petrē,
hēmeis de deisantes apessymeth’·
sentences.l:
And terribly, loudly, he wailed, and round rang the rock,
and we, in fear, rushed away;
sentences.i: He gave a terrible, great cry, and the rock rang round about, and we took fright and rushed away;
sentences.n: σμερδαλέον is an adverb, 'fearfully, terribly', with μέγα 'loudly'. ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω 'wail, cry out in pain'. περὶ δ’ ἴαχε πέτρη 'the rock rang round' shows the echo in the cave, though πέτρη can also mean the crag. ἀπεσσύμεθ’ is ἀπεσσύμεθα, the aorist middle of σεύομαι with ἀπό, 'we rushed away'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ μοχλὸν
ἐξέρυσ’ ὀφθαλμοῖο πεφυρμένον αἵματι πολλῷ.
sentences.tr:
autar ho mochlon
exerys’ ophthalmoio pephyrmenon haimati pollōi.
sentences.l:
but he the stake
pulled out from his eye, smeared with much blood.
sentences.i: but he pulled the stake out of his eye, smeared with a great deal of blood.
sentences.n: ὁ is 'he'. ἐξέρυσ’ is ἐξέρυσε 'pulled out', an aorist of ἐξερύω. ὀφθαλμοῖο is the genitive in -οιο (= -ου), 'from his eye'. πεφυρμένον is the perfect passive participle of φύρω 'mix, soil, smear', agreeing with the stake.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἔρριψεν ἀπὸ ἕο χερσὶν ἀλύων,
αὐτὰρ ὁ Κύκλωπας μεγάλ’ ἤπυεν, οἵ ῥά μιν ἀμφὶς
ᾤκεον ἐν σπήεσσι δι’ ἄκριας ἠνεμοέσσας.
sentences.tr:
ton men epeit’ erripsen apo heo chersin alyōn,
autar ho Kyklōpas megal’ ēpyen, hoi rha min amphis
ōikeon en spēessi di’ akrias ēnemoessas.
sentences.l:
It then he threw from himself with his hands, distraught,
and he the Cyclopes loudly called, who him round about
lived in caves through the windy heights.
sentences.i: Then he flung it away from himself with his hands, beside himself, and called loudly to the Cyclopes, who lived round about him in caves along the windy heights.
sentences.n: τὸν μέν 'it', the stake, is the object of ἔρριψεν 'he flung', the aorist of ῥίπτω, with augment and doubled ρ. ἀπὸ ἕο is 'from himself', ἕο being a genitive of the reflexive pronoun. ἀλύων is 'distraught, beside himself with pain'. ἤπυεν 'called aloud' is from ἠπύω. The relative clause says the Cyclopes live in caves: ᾤκεον is the uncontracted imperfect of οἰκέω, σπήεσσι the dative plural of σπέος 'cave', and ἄκρις is a hill-top or height; ἠνεμοέσσας is 'windy'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ βοῆς ἀίοντες ἐφοίτων ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος,
ἱστάμενοι δ’ εἴροντο περὶ σπέος ὅττι ἑ κήδοι·
sentences.tr:
hoi de boēs aiontes ephoitōn allothen allos,
histamenoi d’ eironto peri speos hotti he kēdoi·
sentences.l:
And they, hearing the shout, came, one from one place, another from another,
and standing round the cave asked what was troubling him;
sentences.i: When they heard his cry they came, one from one place and another from another, and standing round the cave they asked what was troubling him.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ 'and they' is a pronoun. βοῆς takes the genitive, as verbs of hearing do. ἐφοίτων is the imperfect of φοιτάω 'go to and fro, come', here one arrival after another; ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is 'one from here, another from there'. εἴροντο is the Ionic aorist of εἴρομαι 'ask'. ὅττι … κήδοι is an indirect question with the optative, 'what was troubling him'; ἑ is 'him' and κήδω 'distress, trouble'.

sentences.t:
τίπτε τόσον, Πολύφημ’, ἀρημένος ὧδ’ ἐβόησας
νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην καὶ ἀύπνους ἄμμε τίθησθα;
sentences.tr:
tipte toson, Polyphēm’, arēmenos hōd’ eboēsas
nykta di’ ambrosiēn kai aypnous amme tithēstha;
sentences.l:
‘Why so greatly, Polyphemus, distressed, thus did you cry out
through the ambrosial night and sleepless us are you making?
sentences.i: ‘Why, Polyphemus, are you in such distress that you cry out like this through the ambrosial night and keep us from sleep?
sentences.n: A long question, which makes the Cyclopes' speech begin. τίπτε is τί ποτε 'why ever'. ἀρημένος 'distressed, hard-pressed' is a participle whose origin is not clear; the sense is taken from context. ἀμβροσίην is 'ambrosial'. ἄμμε is Aeolic for ἡμᾶς 'us', and ἀύπνους 'sleepless' is the predicate. τίθησθα is the old second-person τίθης in -σθα, 'you make'. Πολύφημ’ is the vocative, with its last vowel dropped.

sentences.t: ἦ μή τίς σευ μῆλα βροτῶν ἀέκοντος ἐλαύνει;
sentences.tr: ē mē tis seu mēla brotōn aekontos elaunei;
sentences.l: Surely not some one of mortals your flocks, you unwilling, is driving off?
sentences.i: Surely no mortal is driving off your flocks against your will?
sentences.n: ἦ μή opens a question that fears the answer: 'surely not'. τίς … βροτῶν is 'any of mortals'. σευ is σου, and ἀέκοντος is a genitive agreeing with the σευ, 'you being unwilling'. The mere 'anyone' here prepares the joke that follows.

sentences.t: ἦ μή τίς σ’ αὐτὸν κτείνει δόλῳ ἠὲ βίηφιν;
sentences.tr: ē mē tis s’ auton kteinei dolōi ēe biēphin;
sentences.l: Surely not some one yourself is killing by trick or by force?’
sentences.i: Surely no one is killing you yourself by a trick or by force?’
sentences.n: Another ἦ μή question. Its μή τίς 'not anyone' has the same sense as the false name Οὖτις (οὔ τις), which Polyphemus will now use in his answer. αὐτόν makes the question personal: 'you yourself'. βίηφιν is βίῃ with the suffix -φιν, 'by force'. The question puts δόλῳ first, 'by a trick', the very weapon used.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ αὖτ’ ἐξ ἄντρου προσέφη κρατερὸς Πολύφημος·
sentences.tr: tous d’ aut’ ex antrou prosephē krateros Polyphēmos·
sentences.l: Them then in turn from the cave addressed strong Polyphemus:
sentences.i: Then strong Polyphemus spoke to them in turn from the cave:
sentences.n: τοὺς is a pronoun, 'them', and the line is a variant of the reply-formula τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε, with προσέφη and a name added. κρατερός 'strong' is the epithet of Polyphemus. ἐξ ἄντρου is 'from the cave'.

sentences.t: ὦ φίλοι, Οὖτίς με κτείνει δόλῳ οὐδὲ βίηφιν.
sentences.tr: ō philoi, Outis me kteinei dolōi oude biēphin.
sentences.l: ‘O friends, Nobody me is killing by trick nor by force.’
sentences.i: ‘Friends, Nobody is killing me by a trick or by force.’
sentences.n: Οὖτις is Nobody, the name Odysseus gave him at the end of the previous part, and it is also the two words οὔ τις 'no one', so what the Cyclopes hear is 'no one is killing me by a trick or by force'. The pun drives the next four lines. δόλῳ οὐδὲ βίηφιν 'by trick nor by force' is a deep irony: it is a trick that is doing it. κτείνει is 'is killing'; ὦ φίλοι is 'friends'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενοι ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευον·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ apameibomenoi epea pteroent’ agoreuon·
sentences.l: And they, answering, winged words spoke:
sentences.i: And in answer they spoke winged words:
sentences.n: οἱ δέ 'and they' is a pronoun. ἀπαμειβόμενοι is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι 'reply'. ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the formula 'winged words', here with the verb ἀγόρευον 'they spoke' (from ἀγορεύω, originally 'speak in the assembly'), and ἀγόρευον is an imperfect without an augment.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ μή τίς σε βιάζεται οἶον ἐόντα,
νοῦσον γ’ οὔ πως ἔστι Διὸς μεγάλου ἀλέασθαι,
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ εὔχεο πατρὶ Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι.
sentences.tr:
ei men dē mē tis se biazetai oion eonta,
nouson g’ ou pōs esti Dios megalou aleasthai,
alla sy g’ eucheo patri Poseidaōni anakti.
sentences.i: ‘If no one is doing you violence while you are alone, there is no way to escape a sickness sent by great Zeus; but pray to your father, lord Poseidon.’
sentences.n: A condition: εἰ … μή τίς σε βιάζεται 'if no one is doing you violence'. The Cyclopes take the false name as a real 'no one' and conclude that the pain is an illness, νοῦσον, the Ionic form of νόσον. Διὸς μεγάλου is 'of great Zeus' (the sender), and ἀλέασθαι is the infinitive of the aorist 'to escape, avoid'. οὔ πως ἔστι is 'it is in no way possible'. πατρί 'to your father' is what the Greek says, and Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι is the house 'lord Poseidon'. They advise prayer to the one god who could help, without knowing that he is the very god Odysseus has offended.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν ἀπιόντες, ἐμὸν δ’ ἐγέλασσε φίλον κῆρ,
ὡς ὄνομ’ ἐξαπάτησεν ἐμὸν καὶ μῆτις ἀμύμων.
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephan apiontes, emon d’ egelasse philon kēr,
hōs onom’ exapatēsen emon kai mētis amymōn.
sentences.l:
So they spoke, going away, and laughed my own dear heart
how my name deceived them, and my cunning, blameless.
sentences.i: So they spoke and went away, and my heart laughed to think how my name had deceived them, and my blameless cunning.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is 'so they spoke'. ἐμὸν … φίλον κῆρ is 'my own dear heart', the Greek way of saying 'I laughed inwardly'. ἐγέλασσε 'laughed' is an aorist with doubled σ. ὡς here is 'how', and ὄνομα καὶ μῆτις 'name and cunning' take a single singular verb, ἐξαπάτησεν, unaugmented. μῆτις is 'cunning intelligence, craft', the quality in πολύμητις, and ἀμύμων is the house 'blameless'; its real meaning is not known. The 'name' is Οὖτις, the false name of the previous part.

sentences.t:
Κύκλωψ δὲ στενάχων τε καὶ ὠδίνων ὀδύνῃσι
χερσὶ ψηλαφόων ἀπὸ μὲν λίθον εἷλε θυράων,
αὐτὸς δ’ εἰνὶ θύρῃσι καθέζετο χεῖρε πετάσσας,
εἴ τινά που μετ’ ὄεσσι λάβοι στείχοντα θύραζε·
sentences.tr:
Kyklōps de stenachōn te kai ōdinōn odynēisi
chersi psēlaphoōn apo men lithon heile thyraōn,
autos d’ eini thyrēisi kathezeto cheire petassas,
ei tina pou met’ oessi laboi steichonta thyraze·
sentences.l:
And the Cyclops, groaning and travailing with pains,
feeling about with his hands, took away the stone from the doors,
and himself in the doorway sat down, hands spreading wide,
if anyone perhaps among the sheep he might catch going out of the door;
sentences.i: The Cyclops, groaning and racked with pain, felt about with his hands and took the stone away from the doors, and sat down himself in the doorway with his arms spread wide, in case he might catch someone going out among the sheep;
sentences.n: A long sentence with two main verbs, εἷλε and καθέζετο, and several participles. ὠδίνων ὀδύνῃσι is 'in travail with pains', the word used of labour-pains. ψηλαφόων 'groping' is uncontracted for ψηλαφῶν. ἀπὸ … εἷλε is 'took away' (tmesis), θυράων a genitive plural in -άων and θύρῃσι a dative plural in -ῃσι; εἰνί is ἐν. χεῖρε is the dual 'his two hands'. The final clause, εἴ … λάβοι 'in case he might catch', has an optative after a past verb, and που is 'perhaps'; μετ’ ὄεσσι is 'among the sheep', ὄεσσι the dative plural of ὄις, and θύραζε '(out) through the door', with the suffix -ζε of direction.

sentences.t: οὕτω γάρ πού μ’ ἤλπετ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ νήπιον εἶναι.
sentences.tr: houtō gar pou m’ ēlpet’ eni phresi nēpion einai.
sentences.l: for so, I suppose, me he expected in his mind foolish to be.
sentences.i: for in his mind he supposed me, I think, to be so foolish.
sentences.n: οὕτω 'so' points back to the trap just described: he sits in the door because he thinks Odysseus is fool enough to walk out by himself. ἤλπετ’ is ἤλπετο, from ἔλπομαι, which in Homer is 'expect, suppose' and is not always 'hope'. πού is 'I suppose'. νήπιον 'foolish' is literally 'not speaking', an infant, and is used of one who does not see what is coming; it recurs at 442.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ βούλευον, ὅπως ὄχ’ ἄριστα γένοιτο,
εἴ τιν’ ἑταίροισιν θανάτου λύσιν ἠδ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ
εὑροίμην·
sentences.tr:
autar egō bouleuon, hopōs och’ arista genoito,
ei tin’ hetairoisin thanatou lysin ēd’ emoi autōi
heuroimēn·
sentences.i: But I was planning how things might turn out by far the best, if I could find some release from death for my companions and for myself;
sentences.n: βούλευον is the imperfect of βουλεύω 'plan' and has no augment. ὅπως … γένοιτο is 'how it might come about', and ὄχα, elided to ὄχ’, is 'by far' with a superlative. εἰ … εὑροίμην 'if I might find' says what the planning hoped for, an optative after a past verb, with εὑροίμην the aorist optative middle of εὑρίσκω. λύσιν is 'release'; ἠδέ is 'and'.

sentences.t:
πάντας δὲ δόλους καὶ μῆτιν ὕφαινον
ὥς τε περὶ ψυχῆς·
sentences.tr:
pantas de dolous kai mētin hyphainon
hōs te peri psychēs·
sentences.l:
and all tricks and cunning I wove,
as when it is for life;
sentences.i: and I wove every kind of trick and cunning, as one does when one’s life is at stake;
sentences.n: ὕφαινον 'I wove' is the ordinary verb for weaving, used here of plotting. δόλους 'tricks' and μῆτιν 'cunning' recall δόλῳ at 408 and μῆτις at 414. ὥς τε περὶ ψυχῆς is 'as (happens) when it is about one's life', and ψυχή here is the life itself, not a ghost.

sentences.t: μέγα γὰρ κακὸν ἐγγύθεν ἦεν.
sentences.tr: mega gar kakon engythen ēen.
sentences.l: for a great evil was near at hand.
sentences.i: for a great evil was close at hand.
sentences.n: ἐγγύθεν has the suffix -θεν, which here gives the sense 'close by'. ἦεν is an epic imperfect of εἰμί, 'was' (Attic ἦν). The line explains why he plots as if for life.

sentences.t: ἥδε δέ μοι κατὰ θυμὸν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλή.
sentences.tr: hēde de moi kata thymon aristē phaineto boulē.
sentences.l: And this, for me, in my heart, appeared the best plan.
sentences.i: And this plan seemed best to me in my heart.
sentences.n: This line appeared in the previous part (318), where it introduced the plan of the stake. Here it introduces the plan of the rams, and the English is the same. ἥδε 'this' points forward; κατὰ θυμόν is 'in my heart'; βουλή is 'plan, counsel'.

sentences.t:
ἄρσενες ὄιες ἦσαν ἐυτρεφέες, δασύμαλλοι,
καλοί τε μεγάλοι τε, ἰοδνεφὲς εἶρος ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
arsenes oies ēsan eytrephees, dasymalloi,
kaloi te megaloi te, iodnephes eiros echontes·
sentences.l:
Male sheep there were, well-fed, thick-fleeced,
fine and big, a violet-dark fleece having;
sentences.i: There were male sheep, well-fed and thick-fleeced, fine and large, with wool of a violet-dark colour;
sentences.n: ἄρσενες ὄιες are 'male sheep'; ὄιες is the nominative plural of ὄις. ἐυτρεφέες 'well-fed' is the uncontracted nominative plural of ἐυτρεφής, and δασύμαλλοι 'thick-fleeced' (δασύς 'thick, shaggy', μαλλός 'wool') is an ordinary compound adjective. Line 425 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short first syllable of ὄιες is counted long in the second foot, and the last syllable of ἐυτρεφέες (with ἐυ- read as two syllables) is counted long at the start of the fifth foot. εἶρος is Ionic for 'wool'. ἰοδνεφές is 'violet-dark', from ἴον 'violet' and a second element (perhaps 'cloud', perhaps 'darkness') whose meaning is not certain. καλοί τε μεγάλοι τε is 'both fine and big'.

sentences.t:
τοὺς ἀκέων συνέεργον ἐυστρεφέεσσι λύγοισιν,
τῇς ἔπι Κύκλωψ εὗδε πέλωρ, ἀθεμίστια εἰδώς,
σύντρεις αἰνύμενος·
sentences.tr:
tous akeōn syneergon eystrepheessi lygoisin,
tēis epi Kyklōps heude pelōr, athemistia eidōs,
syntreis ainymenos·
sentences.i: I silently tied them together, three at a time, with well-twisted withies, on which the monster Cyclops used to sleep, he who knew lawless ways;
sentences.n: τοὺς is 'them', the rams. ἀκέων is 'silently', and συνέεργον is an uncontracted imperfect of συνέργω 'bind together'. λύγοισιν 'withies' are pliant shoots, here twisted (ἐυστρεφέεσσι). τῇς ἔπι 'on which' is a relative with ἔπι following it; τῇς stands for the feminine dative plural 'on which', the withies being the Cyclops' bedding. Κύκλωψ … πέλωρ: πέλωρ is 'monster', a noun in apposition; ἀθεμίστια εἰδώς is 'knowing lawless things', house ἀθεμίστια. σύντρεις αἰνύμενος 'taking three together' goes with the 'I' of συνέεργον, not with the Cyclops: Odysseus took the rams three at a time. αἰνύμενος is from αἴνυμαι 'take'.

sentences.t:
ὁ μὲν ἐν μέσῳ ἄνδρα φέρεσκε,
τὼ δ’ ἑτέρω ἑκάτερθεν ἴτην σώοντες ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
ho men en mesōi andra phereske,
tō d’ heterō hekaterthen itēn sōontes hetairous.
sentences.l:
the one in the middle a man would carry,
and the other two on either side went, saving my companions.
sentences.i: the one in the middle would carry a man, and the other two went along on either side, keeping my companions safe.
sentences.n: The rams go in threes. ὁ μέν is 'the one', a pronoun, answered by τὼ δέ 'the other two', which is in the dual; ἑτέρω is a dual too, and ἴτην is the dual imperfect of εἶμι 'go'. φέρεσκε has the iterative ending -σκε, 'would carry'. σώοντες is the epic participle of σώω, Attic σῴζοντες, 'keeping safe', the two side rams protecting the man in the middle.

sentences.t: τρεῖς δὲ ἕκαστον φῶτ’ ὄιες φέρον·
sentences.tr: treis de hekaston phōt’ oies pheron·
sentences.l: And three sheep carried each man;
sentences.i: And three sheep carried each man;
sentences.n: τρεῖς … ὄιες 'three sheep' is the subject, and ἕκαστον φῶτ’ 'each man' the object, so each man had a ram on either side and one under which he hung. φέρον is the imperfect of φέρω, unaugmented.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε—
ἀρνειὸς γὰρ ἔην μήλων ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἁπάντων,
τοῦ κατὰ νῶτα λαβών, λασίην ὑπὸ γαστέρ’ ἐλυσθεὶς
κείμην·
sentences.tr:
autar egō ge—
arneios gar eēn mēlōn och’ aristos hapantōn,
tou kata nōta labōn, lasiēn hypo gaster’ elystheis
keimēn·
sentences.i: but as for me—there was a ram, by far the best of all the flocks—I took him by the back, curled up under his shaggy belly, and lay there;
sentences.n: The γάρ clause after the dash is a parenthesis, and the sentence then resumes: 'but as for me …' is finished by κείμην, 'I lay', with λαβών and ἐλυσθείς as its participles. ἀρνειός is a ram, here the best ram of all; ἔην is ἦν 'was', and ὄχ’ ἄριστος 'by far best'. τοῦ is a pronoun, 'him'. κατὰ νῶτα λαβών is 'taking him by the back'. ἐλυσθείς is the aorist passive of εἰλύω, here 'curling myself up'. κείμην is ἐκείμην 'I lay', unaugmented. μήλων is the genitive plural of μῆλον 'flock animal'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ χερσὶν ἀώτου θεσπεσίοιο
νωλεμέως στρεφθεὶς ἐχόμην τετληότι θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
autar chersin aōtou thespesioio
nōlemeōs strephtheis echomēn tetlēoti thymōi.
sentences.l:
and with my hands of the fleece, wondrous,
unceasingly, twisting myself, I clung, with enduring heart.
sentences.i: and I clung with my hands to the wondrous fleece, twisting myself round, without letting go, with an enduring heart.
sentences.n: ἀώτου 'of the fleece' is the genitive after ἐχόμην, because ἔχομαι 'hold on to' takes the genitive; θεσπεσίοιο is 'wondrous', a genitive in -οιο. νωλεμέως is 'unceasingly, without a pause'. στρεφθείς 'having twisted myself' most likely refers to his body, curled up under the ram (see ἐλυσθείς at 433). τετληότι θυμῷ is the house 'with an enduring heart'.

sentences.t: ὣς τότε μὲν στενάχοντες ἐμείναμεν Ἠῶ δῖαν.
sentences.tr: hōs tote men stenachontes emeinamen Ēō dian.
sentences.l: So then, indeed, groaning, we waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.i: So then, groaning, we waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.n: The same line as 306 in the previous part, where the men also waited for day; the English is unchanged. μέν and δέ set the night against the morning. Ἠῶ δῖαν 'heavenly Dawn' uses the house δῖος.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτα νομόνδ’ ἐξέσσυτο ἄρσενα μῆλα,
θήλειαι δὲ μέμηκον ἀνήμελκτοι περὶ σηκούς·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
kai tot’ epeita nomond’ exessyto arsena mēla,
thēleiai de memēkon anēmelktoi peri sēkous·
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then the male flocks rushed out to pasture, while the females, unmilked, bleated about the pens;
sentences.n: The first line is the formula for daybreak, also in 307 of the previous part, and the English of its first line is unchanged. νομόνδε is 'to the pasture', with the suffix -δε of direction. ἐξέσσυτο is the aorist of σεύομαι. ἄρσενα μῆλα are the 'male flocks', the rams and he-goats; θήλειαι 'the females' are the ewes and she-goats. μέμηκον is a past form of μηκάομαι 'bleat', either a pluperfect or a reduplicated aorist, and in sense 'were bleating', and ἀνήμελκτοι is 'unmilked'. σηκούς 'pens' is a plural accusative after περί.

sentences.t: οὔθατα γὰρ σφαραγεῦντο.
sentences.tr: outhata gar spharageunto.
sentences.l: for their udders were near bursting.
sentences.i: for their udders were near to bursting.
sentences.n: οὔθατα is 'udders', and γάρ explains the bleating: the ewes were not milked. σφαραγεῦντο is the same verb as at 390, where it was the roots of the eye 'crackling'; it means 'burst with a noise', and here the udders are so swollen that they might burst.

sentences.t:
ἄναξ δ’ ὀδύνῃσι κακῇσι
τειρόμενος πάντων ὀίων ἐπεμαίετο νῶτα
ὀρθῶν ἑσταότων·
sentences.tr:
anax d’ odynēisi kakēisi
teiromenos pantōn oiōn epemaieto nōta
orthōn hestaotōn·
sentences.i: And the lord, worn down by his evil pains, felt over the backs of all the sheep as they stood upright;
sentences.n: ἄναξ 'lord' is the house word and here names Polyphemus as master of the flock. ὀδύνῃσι κακῇσι is a dative of cause, 'by evil pains'. τειρόμενος is the participle of τείρω 'wear down'. ἐπεμαίετο is the imperfect of ἐπιμαίομαι 'feel over, stroke'. ὀρθῶν ἑσταότων is 'standing upright', ἑσταότων being the uncontracted genitive plural of the perfect participle (Attic ἑστώτων).

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ νήπιος οὐκ ἐνόησεν,
ὥς οἱ ὑπ’ εἰροπόκων ὀίων στέρνοισι δέδεντο.
sentences.tr:
to de nēpios ouk enoēsen,
hōs hoi hyp’ eiropokōn oiōn sternoisi dedento.
sentences.l:
but this, foolish, he did not perceive,
how under his wool-bearing sheep, at the chests, they were bound.
sentences.i: but in his foolishness he did not notice this: how the men were tied beneath the chests of his wool-bearing sheep.
sentences.n: τὸ δέ 'but this' is the object of ἐνόησεν 'perceived', and ὥς is 'how'. νήπιος 'foolish' is the same word as at 419. οἱ 'to him' is best taken as 'his' with ὀίων. εἰροπόκων 'wool-bearing' comes from εἶρος 'wool' and a root meaning 'shear'. στέρνοισι is a dative plural in -οισι, and δέδεντο is the pluperfect passive of δέω 'bind'; the subject, the men, is left to be understood.

sentences.t:
ὕστατος ἀρνειὸς μήλων ἔστειχε θύραζε
λάχνῳ στεινόμενος καὶ ἐμοὶ πυκινὰ φρονέοντι.
sentences.tr:
hystatos arneios mēlōn esteiche thyraze
lachnōi steinomenos kai emoi pykina phroneonti.
sentences.l:
Last the ram of the flocks went toward the door,
burdened by the wool and by me, thinking shrewd thoughts.
sentences.i: The ram went last of the flock toward the door, weighed down by his wool and by me, who was thinking shrewd thoughts.
sentences.n: ὕστατος 'last' is the point: the lead ram goes last because of the extra weight. μήλων is 'of the flocks'. θύραζε is 'toward the door', with -ζε. λάχνῳ is a dative of cause, 'by the wool', and στεινόμενος 'weighed down, pressed' is from στείνομαι. πυκινά is 'shrewd' (literally 'close-packed, dense'), and φρονέοντι is the uncontracted participle of φρονέω, in the dative because it agrees with ἐμοί 'me'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπιμασσάμενος προσέφη κρατερὸς Πολύφημος·
sentences.tr: ton d’ epimassamenos prosephē krateros Polyphēmos·
sentences.l: Him then, having felt over, addressed strong Polyphemus:
sentences.i: Then strong Polyphemus felt over him and spoke to him:
sentences.n: A second introduction in the style of the reply-formulas, here without 'in turn', for no one has spoken. ἐπιμασσάμενος is the aorist participle of ἐπιμαίομαι, the same verb as ἐπεμαίετο at 441, 'having felt over'. κρατερός is 'strong', as at 407.

sentences.t:
κριὲ πέπον, τί μοι ὧδε διὰ σπέος ἔσσυο μήλων
ὕστατος;
sentences.tr:
krie pepon, ti moi hōde dia speos essyo mēlōn
hystatos;
sentences.l:
‘Good ram, why, for me, thus through the cave have you rushed, of the flocks
last?
sentences.i: ‘My good ram, why have you rushed through the cave like this, last of the flock?
sentences.n: Polyphemus speaks to the ram as to a companion. πέπον is a familiar form of address in the vocative; its exact sense ('ripe', 'soft', 'dear') is not known, and 'good' is the nearest plain word. κριέ is 'ram'. τί μοι is 'why, for me'. ἔσσυο is the second-person aorist middle of σεύομαι, 'you have rushed', which is how a ram ought to leave the cave, and the reverse of how this ram does. ὧδε is 'thus', and μήλων is 'of the flocks'.

sentences.t:
οὔ τι πάρος γε λελειμμένος ἔρχεαι οἰῶν,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρῶτος νέμεαι τέρεν’ ἄνθεα ποίης
μακρὰ βιβάς,
sentences.tr:
ou ti paros ge leleimmenos ercheai oiōn,
alla poly prōtos nemeai teren’ anthea poiēs
makra bibas,
sentences.l:
Never before, at least, left behind do you go of the sheep,
but far first you graze the tender flowers of the grass,
striding long,
sentences.i: You never used to go behind the sheep; you were always first by far to graze the tender flowers of the grass, striding on with long steps,
sentences.n: οὔ τι πάρος γε is 'not at all before'. λελειμμένος is 'left behind', a perfect passive participle, with οἰῶν 'behind the sheep' in the genitive, as after a verb of falling short (οἰῶν is the contracted genitive plural of ὄις). ἔρχεαι is the uncontracted second-person middle 'you go'. νέμεαι is 'you graze on', also uncontracted. τέρεν’ is τέρενα 'tender', and ποίης is 'of the grass', Ionic η. μακρὰ βιβάς is 'striding long', the participle of βίβημι and μακρά an adverbial neuter plural.

sentences.t:
πρῶτος δὲ ῥοὰς ποταμῶν ἀφικάνεις,
πρῶτος δὲ σταθμόνδε λιλαίεαι ἀπονέεσθαι
ἑσπέριος·
sentences.tr:
prōtos de rhoas potamōn aphikaneis,
prōtos de stathmonde lilaieai aponeesthai
hesperios·
sentences.i: you were first to reach the running streams of the rivers, and first, in the evening, you longed to go back to the stall;
sentences.n: ῥοάς 'streams' is the object of ἀφικάνεις 'you arrive at', a longer form of ἀφικνέομαι. σταθμόνδε is 'to the stall' (-δε). λιλαίεαι is 'you long for', uncontracted, governing the infinitive ἀπονέεσθαι 'to go back', also uncontracted. ἑσπέριος is an adjective used like an adverb, 'in the evening'. The three πρῶτος in three lines (449, 450, 451) build the contrast with πανύστατος.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖτε πανύστατος.
sentences.tr: nyn aute panystatos.
sentences.l: now again the very last.
sentences.i: now you are the very last.
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτε 'now, on the other hand' turns the list round. πανύστατος 'very last, last of all' is ὕστατος (448) strengthened with πάν-. The unit is a half-line.

sentences.t:
ἦ σύ γ’ ἄνακτος
ὀφθαλμὸν ποθέεις, τὸν ἀνὴρ κακὸς ἐξαλάωσε
σὺν λυγροῖς ἑτάροισι δαμασσάμενος φρένας οἴνῳ,
Οὖτις, ὃν οὔ πώ φημι πεφυγμένον εἶναι ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
ē sy g’ anaktos
ophthalmon potheeis, ton anēr kakos exalaōse
syn lygrois hetaroisi damassamenos phrenas oinōi,
Outis, hon ou pō phēmi pephygmenon einai olethron.
sentences.l:
Surely you, at least, for your lord’s
eye yearn, which a base man put out
with grievous companions, having overpowered my wits with wine,
Nobody, whom not yet I say to have escaped destruction.
sentences.i: Surely you are longing for your lord’s eye, which a base man put out together with his grievous companions, after overpowering my wits with wine — Nobody, who, I say, has not yet escaped destruction.
sentences.n: ἦ σύ γε asserts 'surely you'. ἄνακτος is 'of your lord', the Cyclops speaking of himself as the ram's master. ποθέεις is 'you miss, long for'. The man is ἀνὴρ κακός, 'a base man'. λυγροῖς is the house 'grievous', which makes an odd epithet for people, but follows the table. δαμασσάμενος φρένας οἴνῳ is 'overpowering my wits with wine'. Οὖτις is in apposition to ἀνήρ, 'Nobody', and ὅν is the relative 'whom'. πεφυγμένον εἶναι ὄλεθρον 'to have escaped destruction' is the periphrastic perfect infinitive, the perfect participle πεφυγμένον with εἶναι; the Cyclops is right without knowing it, for the man he means is clinging under the ram beneath his hand.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὴ ὁμοφρονέοις ποτιφωνήεις τε γένοιο
εἰπεῖν ὅππῃ κεῖνος ἐμὸν μένος ἠλασκάζει·
sentences.tr:
ei dē homophroneois potiphōnēeis te genoio
eipein hoppēi keinos emon menos ēlaskazei·
sentences.l:
If only you were of one mind and became able to speak,
to tell where that one is skulking from my strength;
sentences.i: If only you felt as I do and could find a voice, to tell me where that man is lurking to avoid my strength;
sentences.n: A wish put as a condition, εἰ with the optative: ὁμοφρονέοις 'you were of one mind' and γένοιο 'you became' are optatives. ποτιφωνήεις is 'able to speak to', from ποτί (= πρός) and φωνή 'voice', the only use in this part. εἰπεῖν ὅππῃ is 'to say where'. κεῖνος is 'that one'. ἠλασκάζει is 'wanders about, skulks', and with ἐμὸν μένος as its object, 'my strength', it is taken to mean 'slinks away from, shuns'.

sentences.t:
τῷ κέ οἱ ἐγκέφαλός γε διὰ σπέος ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ
θεινομένου ῥαίοιτο πρὸς οὔδεϊ, κὰδ δέ κ’ ἐμὸν κῆρ
λωφήσειε κακῶν, τά μοι οὐτιδανὸς πόρεν Οὖτις.
sentences.tr:
tōi ke hoi enkephalos ge dia speos allydis allēi
theinomenou rhaioito pros oudeï, kad de k’ emon kēr
lōphēseie kakōn, ta moi outidanos poren Outis.
sentences.l:
then his brain, through the cave, here and there,
as he is struck, would be dashed against the floor, and down my heart
would rest from the evils which a worthless Nobody gave me.’
sentences.i: then his brains would be dashed against the floor all through the cave, this way and that, as he was struck, and my heart would be eased of the evils that worthless Nobody has given me.’
sentences.n: The other half of the wish. τῷ is 'in that case', and the optatives with κε, ῥαίοιτο and λωφήσειε, say what would follow: 'would be dashed', 'would rest'. οἱ … θεινομένου is 'his … as he was struck', the genitive of θείνω 'strike'. ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ is 'this way and that'. ῥαίοιτο is the optative of ῥαίω 'shatter'. κὰδ is κατά with its last vowel lost, and its exact force with λωφήσειε 'rest, abate' is unclear; it is taken to mean 'be eased'. πόρεν is the aorist of πορεῖν 'give', unaugmented. οὐτιδανός is 'worthless', a word very like Οὖτις that may well be a pun on it.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν τὸν κριὸν ἀπὸ ἕο πέμπε θύραζε.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn ton krion apo heo pempe thyraze.
sentences.l: So having spoken, the ram from himself he sent away to the door.
sentences.i: With that he sent the ram away from him, out through the door.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken'. τὸν κριόν is 'the ram' (a different word from ἀρνειός, which is the same animal). ἀπὸ ἕο is 'from himself', as at 398. πέμπε is ἔπεμπε 'sent', with no augment.

sentences.t:
ἐλθόντες δ’ ἠβαιὸν ἀπὸ σπείους τε καὶ αὐλῆς
πρῶτος ὑπ’ ἀρνειοῦ λυόμην, ὑπέλυσα δ’ ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
elthontes d’ ēbaion apo speious te kai aulēs
prōtos hyp’ arneiou lyomēn, hypelysa d’ hetairous.
sentences.l:
And when we had gone a little from the cave and the yard,
first from under the ram I loosed myself, and I loosed my companions.
sentences.i: When we had gone a little way from the cave and the yard, I was the first to free myself from under the ram, and then I freed my companions.
sentences.n: ἐλθόντες 'having gone' is plural: the whole party, men and rams. ἠβαιόν is 'a little', an adverb, and σπείους is the genitive of σπέος 'cave'. αὐλῆς is 'yard', as in the previous part. λυόμην is the middle 'I freed myself' and ὑπέλυσα the active 'I freed from underneath'; πρῶτος 'first' is the point of the sentence.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δὲ τὰ μῆλα ταναύποδα, πίονα δημῷ,
πολλὰ περιτροπέοντες ἐλαύνομεν, ὄφρ’ ἐπὶ νῆα
ἱκόμεθ’.
sentences.tr:
karpalimōs de ta mēla tanaupoda, piona dēmōi,
polla peritropeontes elaunomen, ophr’ epi nēa
hikometh’.
sentences.l:
And swiftly the flocks, long-footed, fat with fat,
often turning, we drove, until to the ship
we came.
sentences.i: We quickly drove the long-legged flocks, fat with fat, turning about again and again, until we reached the ship.
sentences.n: μῆλα ταναύποδα, πίονα δημῷ is 'flocks, long-footed, fat with fat'; ταναύποδα is 'long-footed', from the root of τανύω 'stretch', and the exact sense ('with stretched legs', 'long-legged') is not certain. πίονα is the 'fat' of πίονα μῆλα. περιτροπέοντες is a rare verb, 'turning about'; whether they looked behind them or turned the animals about is not known, and the plain word is used. πολλά is taken as an adverb, 'often'. ἐλαύνομεν is 'we drove'. ὄφρα is 'until', and ἱκόμεθ’ is ἱκόμεθα, the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι.

sentences.t:
ἀσπάσιοι δὲ φίλοις ἑτάροισι φάνημεν,
οἳ φύγομεν θάνατον, τοὺς δὲ στενάχοντο γοῶντες.
sentences.tr:
aspasioi de philois hetaroisi phanēmen,
hoi phygomen thanaton, tous de stenachonto goōntes.
sentences.l:
And welcome to our dear companions we appeared,
we who had escaped death, but for those they groaned, lamenting.
sentences.i: We were a welcome sight to our dear companions, we who had escaped death; but for the others they groaned aloud, lamenting.
sentences.n: ἀσπάσιοι 'welcome' agrees with the 'we' of φάνημεν, the aorist passive of φαίνω, 'appeared'. φύγομεν is the aorist of φεύγω, unaugmented. The last clause, τοὺς δὲ, is 'and for those', meaning the men eaten by the Cyclops; στενάχοντο is 'groaned' and γοῶντες is the participle of γοάω 'wail, lament'. The men on the ship mourn for their dead, and the joy is mixed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ εἴων, ἀνὰ δ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦον ἑκάστῳ,
κλαίειν, ἀλλ’ ἐκέλευσα θοῶς καλλίτριχα μῆλα
πόλλ’ ἐν νηὶ βαλόντας ἐπιπλεῖν ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
all’ egō ouk eiōn, ana d’ ophrysi neuon hekastōi,
klaiein, all’ ekeleusa thoōs kallitricha mēla
poll’ en nēi balontas epiplein halmyron hydōr.
sentences.l:
But I did not allow—and with my brows I nodded up to each—
to weep, but I bade them quickly the fair-coated flocks
many in the ship having thrown, to sail over the salt water.
sentences.i: But I would not let them weep, and I signalled to each man with raised brows not to, and told them instead to throw the many fair-coated flocks quickly into the ship and to sail over the salt water.
sentences.n: οὐκ εἴων is 'I did not allow', the imperfect of ἐάω. The clause ἀνὰ δ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦον ἑκάστῳ is thrown in: νεῦον is 'I nodded', and ἀνά with it gives 'upward', a refusal made by raising the brows; the Greek sign for 'no' was an upward movement. κλαίειν 'to weep' is the infinitive that goes with εἴων. καλλίτριχα μῆλα is the house 'fair-coated flocks'. πόλλ’ is πολλά, agreeing with μῆλα, and βαλόντας is 'having thrown', with ἐν νηί 'in the ship' meaning 'into the ship' after a verb of throwing. ἐπιπλεῖν ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ is 'sail over the salt water', with ἁλμυρός 'salty'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον,
ἑξῆς δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aips’ eisbainon kai epi klēisi kathizon,
hexēs d’ hezomenoi poliēn hala typton eretmois.
sentences.l:
And they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down,
and sitting in a row, the grey sea they struck with their oars.
sentences.i: They quickly went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks, and sitting in rows, they struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: The same two lines as 103 of odyssey-039 (the second is also found elsewhere); the English is unchanged. εἴσβαινον 'went aboard' and καθῖζον 'sat down' are imperfects with no augment, and ἐπὶ κληῖσι is 'on the rowing-benches'. ἑξῆς is 'in order, in a row', and πολιὴν ἅλα is the house 'the grey sea'; ἐρετμοῖς is 'with oars'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε τόσσον ἀπῆν, ὅσσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼ Κύκλωπα προσηύδων κερτομίοισι·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote tosson apēn, hosson te gegōne boēsas,
kai tot’ egō Kyklōpa prosēudōn kertomioisi·
sentences.l:
But when so far off it was as one shouting makes himself heard,
and then I to the Cyclops spoke with taunting ones:
sentences.i: But when we were as far off as a man’s shout can carry, then I spoke to the Cyclops with taunts:
sentences.n: The first line is also found in an earlier part (a different speaker there), and the wording is kept. ἀπῆν is 'was away', a singular verb whose subject, presumably the ship, is not stated; the sense is 'when we were that far away'. ὅσσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας is 'as far as a man makes himself heard shouting', γέγωνε being a perfect with present sense. προσηύδων is 'I spoke to', the imperfect of προσαυδάω. κερτομίοισι is 'taunting, cutting', a dative agreeing with an understood 'words'. The ano teleia, rendered as a colon, promises a speech, which this part does not reach.
